blocks.p: It's 9:15 at night. You finally sat down to meditate. Ten seconds in, your worry list is louder than it's been all day, your shoulders are up around your ears, and you've already decided (again) that you're just bad at this.
But maybe you're not bad at it.
Maybe the instruction was wrong. "Clear your mind" and "just be still" ask your body to do something it can't do on command, especially when it doesn't feel safe yet.

blocks.h: What nervous system meditation actually is

blocks.p: The way we do things in [the Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) is different. Yes, we meditate. But the instruction is much different. And so is the goal.
Our goal is to connect with the felt sense of the present moment, both internal and external, no matter what they bring.

ul: External present moment: mindfully using our senses to connect with sights, sounds, and textures outside of the body.
Internal present moment: mindfully using our conscious awareness to connect with the array of thoughts, feelings, sensations, and even impulses within us.

blocks.p: When we connect with the present moment externally, we can then gradually connect with the internal. The external world connection allows simple mindfulness and a gentle connection with safety. This anchors the nervous system and opens the potential to explore more deeply, eventually allowing deep self-regulation at the nervous system level.

This meditation goal isn't an empty head or a perfectly still body. The goal is to notice the present moment and stay with it; to connect with what's actually happening in your breath and body here and now. That's it.
The stillness, when it comes, if it comes, is the result, not the task.
Your body can shift state on its own; we just need to pay attention to it and let the process unfold. Force and control are the enemies of nervous-system-level meditation.

blocks.h3: There are no hacks to nervous system level meditation

blocks.p: This type of meditation is not forced. Instead, we gently connect with the body's state as it naturally is.

The gentle connection is only as strong as your safety state allows, however. The stronger your safety state, the greater your connection to the present moment and your capacity to welcome whatever surfaces. This is essential, as nervous-system-level meditation requires you to connect with defensive activation, even long-held ones. Maybe not the first time. But eventually.

There are no hacks to build the safety state. That comes from daily practices, like those found in Stuck Not Broken: Book 2 or in Stage 2 of the [Unstucking Pathway](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator).
One thing that may help settle the system is an extended exhale. Stephen Porges, the creator of the Polyvagal Theory, says:

q: The most direct way to access the neural pathway that turns off threat is through breathing, exhaling slowly.

blocks.p: I don't recommend controlled breathing for the most part, but I find benefit in one intentional breath in and out. After that one breath, I recommend focusing on the body's natural breathing.

Why? Because if you're not focusing on the natural rhythm, then you're focusing on counting. And if you're doing that, then you're more concerned with executing the skill correctly. And if you're more concerned about proper execution, then you're less connected with the present moment within and without yourself.
We focus on what is true in the present moment as much as possible.

If you rely on controlled breath, that's fine for now. As you practice, see if you're more curious about your body's natural breath. To exit a stuck defensive state, you eventually need to let your body be in that stuck state, then exit it. And that means your natural breath changes along with the stuck state's presence.

During this one intentional breath and beyond, you don't have to believe anything or empty anything, sit in any specific way or on any specific thing. You just give the exhale a little more time than the inhale.
There are no hacks or shortcuts. And quality matters much more than quantity.
Yeah, you can follow your favorite app's guided meditation and try to fight your thoughts for 30 minutes. And that's maybe something.
But I think you'd get more out of 30 seconds of connecting with your senses and taking an intentional breath. Which of these two would you prefer?

ol: Try not to think for 30 minutes while sitting with folded legs and your eyes closed.
Spend 30 seconds sipping a warm tea, looking out a window at the breeze in the leaves, noticing your breath, and acknowledging a pain you're carrying.

blocks.p: To be fair, neither of the above two options is sufficient on its own for re-regulating at the nervous system level. But option 2 sets you up much better for that level of work. As the thirty seconds become easier, you can extend the practice longer and deeper.

Present-moment self-connection is the whole point: not escaping the moment, not improving it, just being in it with your own body for a little while. When you reject the moment you're in through wishing it were calmer, quieter, or that you were further along, you have left the practice. This is completely okay and expected.
Just try again later, remaining open to the external and internal present.

If you've ever tried to sit perfectly still and felt more wound up, that's not your imagination. When your body is not in its safety state, being told to immobilize can read as a threat, not a rest, even if no literal threat is present. That's why "just relax" so often does the opposite.

Immobilization that actually settles you is something your system eases into once it has a few [cues of safety](piece:polyvagal-safety). When immobilization combines with enough safety, the result is the mixed autonomic state of stillness. Sympathetic flight/fight needs to be turned down in order for stillness to emerge.

How do you get more safety in your system? A slow exhale is one of those cues. As is a view out a window. Maybe silence. And maybe a warm tea. It depends on your wonderful nervous system. You will need to listen to what feels better than not. The environment is a great place to start.
Altering your environment is a significant piece of safety, but not the entire answer.

Your Passive Safety Environment is different than mine and the next person's, so you'll need to listen to how your system responds to various sensory inputs. In the Safety Simplified cohort, I recommend students choose one environment in their home, then make minor adjustments to it, like removing clutter or adding something pleasant to hold onto.
After you adjust your environment in minor ways, practice connecting to the present moment with simple mindfulness, as we do in live Mindful Moments (available at no cost to all).

blocks.h: An easy, two-minute nervous system meditation for beginners

blocks.p: Let's make nervous-system-level meditation more real. And make it more simple.
One practice. Two minutes. Do it when you know you're most likely to be successful.

ol: Sit, lie, stand, or lean wherever you feel best. (The Passive Safety Environment is ideal.)
Take one intentional big breath in and let it out slowly.
Follow your body's natural breathing rhythm.
Then, focus on your senses and what they are drawn to in the environment.
Notice what helps your body settle more and focus your senses on that one thing.
Identify where safety lives in your body.
Acknowledge an easy but uncomfortable emotion (like annoyance).
Notice where that emotion lives in your body for a second.
Bring your attention back to safety in your body.
Bring your attention back to the external environment.

blocks.p: This practice takes about two minutes. It's not much, but it's the start of a deeper meditative practice at the nervous system level. And it has the bones of what's necessary:

blocks.why: The same bones as these two minutes: your senses, your natural breath, and safety in your body. Tuned to you.

blocks.p: This won't empty your mind. Minds don't empty; they wander, and a wandering mind is not a failed meditation. It's just a wandering mind. No more. No less. Instead of fighting it, acknowledge it.
It won't make a hard day stop being hard. But it might make it more emotionally manageable. And maybe you can think more clearly about what needs to be handled.

If you want to know which state you're actually in before you practice, start with [how to read your own nervous system](hub:read). And if you'd like a daily place to practice alongside other people doing the same work, that's what the [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) is for.

blocks.h3: Is nervous system meditation different from regular meditation?

blocks.p: It looks similar from the outside, but the goal is different. The goal with meditating at a nervous system level is to connect with the body's felt sense, regardless of what is present. Typical meditation focuses on how the practice should be, not what truly is.

blocks.h3: Why does meditation sometimes make me more anxious?

blocks.p: Because immobilizing is a cue of danger for someone stuck in a defensive state. Flight and fight needs space and movement, not immobility.

blocks.h3: How long should I meditate to regulate my nervous system?

blocks.p: Two minutes done daily beats twenty minutes done once. Short and repeatable is what builds the pattern and sustainable success. Consistency matters more than length, especially at the start.

blocks.h3: Do I have to clear my mind?

blocks.p: No. Minds wander because minds wander. Notice where your attention went and bring it to the next breath as you can. This is normal and reduces over time.

blocks.h3: Can meditation replace therapy for trauma?

blocks.p: Not exactly, no. Meditation is essential for a deep level of self-regulation at the nervous system level, whether practiced solo or guided, as in the [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) and the Skills Sequence in [Stuck Not Broken: Book 3](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/books). But this process only opens to someone with a strong baseline of safety. Therapy can help someone reach that baseline and regulate out of a traumatized state as well.

blocks.h3: What if I can't feel my breath or my body?

blocks.p: That's common, especially after a long stretch of stress or with a low safety baseline. Focus on simple sensory mindfulness first.
